articles.title: My headless agent can now get UI when it needs one
articles.excerpt: I like to work on what my agent does avoiding UI headaches so that I can lazer focus on service capability. A headless agent runs in a terminal or an IDE with no UI. The moment it needs something from…
articles.body: I like to work on what my agent does avoiding UI headaches so that I can lazer focus on service capability. A headless agent runs in a terminal or an IDE with no UI. The moment it needs something from a person it's stuck with a text prompt in the window it's running in, and I have to screencap it and send it via slack/email to others. So I've been building a third option, the agent asks, and the UI appears. Agent describes what it needs: title, inputs, some fields and buttons. It gets back a link to a real page. A person opens it on any device, answers and the agent gets responses back. No frontend in the repo, nothing to design, host or maintain. Demo I picked the case that's easiest to feel for a dev.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Neon vs Carbon vs Hydrogen vs Argon: Hydrogen Answers Twice as Fast, Neon Costs the Most
articles.excerpt: The short answer: use Gemini 4 Hydrogen for agent loops and bulk coding. For answers of 1,500 to 4,000 tokens it took a median 23 seconds on our platform, against 44 for Argon and 49 for Carbon, and a…
articles.body: The short answer: use Gemini 4 Hydrogen for agent loops and bulk coding. For answers of 1,500 to 4,000 tokens it took a median 23 seconds on our platform, against 44 for Argon and 49 for Carbon, and at $0.825 / $4.125 per 1M tokens it is the lowest-priced. Use Gemini 4 Argon when unsure and Gemini 4 Carbon for the hardest debugging. Gemini 4 Neon tops the coding-agent index but costs $3 / $15; on low thinking it cost half as much in our test. In about six weeks Google released four Gemini 4 models: the flagship Argon, announced on 30 September and on the API from 13 October; Carbon, opened to all paid developers on 10 November; Hydrogen on 12 November; and Neon on 18 November. The names are all chemical elements, which tells you nothing about speed or price.

articles.body: This guide first appeared on usewrit.app . I build Writ, the tool in the last part; the first three methods need nothing from us. A supplier updates a price list. A competitor quietly changes its pricing page. A school publishes its admission dates, a status page flips to "degraded", a job board posts the role you were waiting for. In every case the information was public, and in every case you found out late, because nobody tells you when a web page changes. This guide covers the ways to monitor a website for changes, what each one costs you in time, and how to set up an alert that fires only when the part you care about moves. First, decide what "changed" means Almost every page changes on every load: a date in the footer, a rotating banner, a visitor counter, an ad.

articles.title: Expiring Untagged ECR Images Deletes the Digest an ECS Service Still Runs, and New Tasks Fail to Pull
articles.excerpt: Originally published on KBY Technologies. If you run services on ECS and use ECR lifecycle rules to keep a registry tidy, this is the check we would run before your next cleanup-rule change: whether a…
articles.body: Originally published on KBY Technologies . If you run services on ECS and use ECR lifecycle rules to keep a registry tidy, this is the check we would run before your next cleanup-rule change: whether any service is pinned to a digest that has lost its tag. We cover the read-only commands that confirm it and the order for a safe fix. Symptom New Amazon ECS tasks stop with CannotPullContainerError: pull image manifest has been retried 5 time(s): failed to resolve ref , while the tasks that were already running stay healthy. If the Amazon ECR lifecycle rules changed recently, check first for a rule that expires untagged images. The service is pinned to an image digest, that digest lost its tag when the pipeline pushed a newer image under the same tag, and the rule then deleted it.

articles.excerpt: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours,…
articles.body: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.

articles.body: The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it. The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off. Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light. The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history.
